title: The Accuser Asks for a Test
sum: Isaac is weaned, and Abraham holds a feast. Sarah sees Ishmael playing and dancing while Abraham rejoices, and she grows jealous. The Lord tells Abraham to listen to her, and Hagar and the boy are sent into the desert of Beersheba, where an angel shows Hagar a well. Ishmael grows up an archer and marries an Egyptian.

Then the book does something Genesis does not. Voices in heaven praise Abraham's faithfulness, and Prince Mastema answers that Abraham loves Isaac more than anything: let God tell him to offer Isaac and see. The Lord already knows Abraham has passed every test. The chapter ends with a list of those trials, the start of the book's count of ten.
readings: Read as a retelling of Genesis 21-22

Most of the chapter follows Genesis 21:8-21 closely. The changes clear Ishmael of blame, give Sarah a motive, and above all explain the puzzling first line of Genesis 22, "God put Abraham to the test": the test was the accuser's idea.
Read beside Job

The heavenly scene is built like Job 1-2: praise of a righteous man, an accuser's challenge, a test God allows. Jubilees brings the two books together, so that Abraham becomes the first Job and Mastema the first accuser.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale as Scripture, and so receives this chapter as the account, given on Sinai, of why Abraham was tested.
views.H: Historical critics see a writer of the 100s BC solving problems in Genesis: why God would test a man he knew, and why the good Ishmael was sent away. Moving the test's origin to Mastema protects God from the charge of cruelty, the same move Chronicles makes when Satan, not the LORD, incites David (1 Chronicles 21:1; 2 Samuel 24:1).
views.N: James 1:13 says God "tempts no one himself", and Hebrews 11:17 says Abraham offered Isaac "when God put him to the test." Jubilees shows a Jewish way of holding both: God permits a test that the accuser proposes. Matthew 4:1 has the same shape in Jesus' testing by the devil.
views.J: The rabbis tell a similar story: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 89b reads Genesis 22:1 "after these things" as "after the words of Satan", who complains about Abraham before God. Mishnah Avot 5:3 counts ten trials of Abraham.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early Jewish answer to a real question in Genesis 22, worth knowing but not binding. Genesis itself says God tested Abraham and gives no heavenly scene.

deep.b:
Genesis 22:1 says plainly that God tested Abraham. Jubilees keeps God in control but puts the request in Mastema's mouth (17:16). The pattern is old: in Job 1-2 the LORD allows the accuser to test Job, and in 1 Chronicles 21:1 Satan incites David where 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD did. The book returns to this move again and again: Mastema, not God, attacks Moses on the way to Egypt (48:2-3), and the powers of Mastema kill the firstborn (49:2).

The Qumran text 4Q225, called Pseudo-Jubilees, has the same opening: in Fitzmyer's translation, "The Prince Mastemah came to God and lodged a complaint against Abraham about Isaac." Fitzmyer cites the line as fragment 2, column i, lines 9-10. A copy of that text was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls; whether it was composed there is not shown.

17:17 lists the earlier trials: leaving his land, famine, the wealth of kings, Sarah taken by force, circumcision, and Ishmael and Hagar sent away. The text itself numbers only the last: the burial of Sarah is "the tenth trial" (19:8). The full count is Charles's: he takes the sending away of Ishmael and of Hagar as two trials, the sixth and seventh, and adds Sarah's barrenness and the binding of Isaac as the eighth and ninth, which he says are "not specifically reckoned as such in our text". The Mishnah's "ten trials" (Mishnah Avot 5:3) gives no list; later lists differ. The point of 17:17-18 is that the coming test adds nothing to what God knows. It shows the accuser, and the reader, what Abraham is.

echoes: Genesis 21:8-21; Genesis 22:1; Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-6; 1 Chronicles 21:1; James 1:13; Hebrews 11:17; Romans 9:7; Galatians 4:21-31

settings.when: at the feast for Isaac's weaning, after watching Ishmael play
settings.why: To keep the inheritance for Isaac alone. Jubilees makes it plain that she speaks from jealousy, not because Ishmael did wrong.
To settle that the promised line runs through Isaac, while promising that Ishmael too will become a great nation.

settings.by: an angel of God, one of the holy ones
settings.why: To rescue the boy and assure Hagar that the Lord had heard her.

settings.when: the 12th of the first month, after voices in heaven praised Abraham
settings.why: To accuse Abraham of loving Isaac more than God and to force a test. Inside the story it is a charge to be answered; for readers it explains why a good God would ask such a thing.
settings.readers: A copy of the Qumran text 4Q225, which tells the same scene (fragment 2, column i, lines 9-10, in Fitzmyer's citation), was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the scene was copied there.

title: The Binding of Isaac
sum: The Lord tells Abraham to take his beloved son Isaac to the high land and offer him on a mountain. The story follows Genesis 22 closely: the early start, the third day, the servants left behind, the wood on Isaac's back, the question about the lamb, the altar and the knife.

But now the angel who tells the story stands beside Abraham, and Prince Mastema stands watching. The Lord sends the angel to stop the knife, and Mastema is put to shame. The place is named "The Lord Has Seen" and identified as Mount Zion. The oath of blessing follows, and Abraham keeps a seven-day festival every year to remember the journey, a law written on the heavenly tablets.
readings: Read as a contest

In Jubilees the binding is a trial of strength between Abraham's faithfulness and Mastema's accusation. The test ends not with Abraham's relief but with the accuser's shame (18:12), and the Lord makes Abraham's faith known "to all" (18:16).
Read as the origin of a feast and a place

The story ends with a mountain (Zion, 18:13) and a feast (18:18-19). For a priestly writer, the place of the Temple and its sacrifices goes back to the binding of Isaac, and Israel's festival goes back to Abraham's journey.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale as Scripture, together with the Orit (the books of Moses), where Genesis 22 tells the same story.
views.H: Critics note the writer's priestly interests: the mountain is Zion, the ram is offered there, and a seven-day festival is founded. Fitzmyer notes that the dates (17:15; 18:3) bring Abraham to the mountain on the fifteenth of the first month, "when Passover was being celebrated", so that the book "may connect the sacrifice of Isaac with Passover, but only indirectly" (see the section below).
views.N: Hebrews 11:17-19 and James 2:21-23 both use the binding to speak of Abraham's faith, as Jubilees does, and Hebrews reads his "we will come back" as faith in resurrection. Christians have long read Isaac carrying the wood and the ram given in his place as pictures of Christ (John 1:29; Romans 8:32).
views.J: The Akedah became central in Jewish prayer and thought. The Qumran text 4Q225 retells it with Mastemah, weeping angels and Isaac asking to be bound, as Fitzmyer's translation shows; Fitzmyer notes that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan also has Isaac ask to be bound well.
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 22 as the authoritative account and find Jubilees useful as a window on how Jews of the second century BC understood it, especially the question of why God tested Abraham.

deep.b: Most of 18:1-17 is Genesis 22:1-19, with small changes in wording that often match the Septuagint: "your beloved son" for "your only one" (18:2), "the high land" for "the land of Moriah" (18:2), "cities" for "gate" (18:15). The additions are few but they change the story: a well (18:4), the knife in Isaac's question (18:6), the narrator and Mastema standing by (18:9), Abraham's terror (18:10), Mastema put to shame (18:12), the mountain named as Zion (18:13), the angels explained as speaking in the Lord's name (18:14), and the festival (18:18-19).

The fragment 4Q225 (called Pseudo-Jubilees) tells the binding with even more figures. In Fitzmyer's translation of fragment 2, holy angels stand "weeping over the altar", the angels of Mastemah rejoice and say "Now he will perish", Isaac asks his father to "Bind me fast", and a broken line begins "The prince Mastemah bound". Fitzmyer warns that the text is fragmentary "just at the points where one finds the different distinctive elements", so each detail is partly restored. Jubilees has none of these, but the two texts share the core: Mastemah's complaint (fragment 2, column i, lines 9-10) and his defeat.

The voices in heaven speak "in the first month of this jubilee, on the twelfth of that month" (17:15). Abraham sets out early the next morning and sees the place "on the third day" (18:3). Fitzmyer counts that as the fifteenth day, "when Passover was being celebrated", and concludes that Jubilees "may connect the sacrifice of Isaac with Passover, but only indirectly": the reader is left to add the three days. In Leviticus the Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread begins on the fifteenth and lasts seven days (Leviticus 23:5-6). Abraham's own festival also lasts seven days (18:18), though the book explains them as the days of his journey there and back and never names the feast.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the provided lamb and the Passover lamb
deep.b: If the writer did mean the link with Passover, the lamb the Lord would "see to" on the mountain (18:7) and the Passover lamb meet in one season. Christian readers who see Christ as both the Lamb of God (John 1:29) and the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7) would find the two already joined in a Jewish book.

echoes: Genesis 22:1-19; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Job 1:6-12; Hebrews 11:17-19; James 2:21-23; Romans 8:32; John 1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Leviticus 23:5-8

settings.why: To test Abraham before the accuser. In Jubilees the reader already knows the outcome (17:17-18), so the command reads as a demonstration rather than a trap.

settings.to: his two young servants, at a well
settings.when: on the third day, with the place in sight
settings.why: To leave them behind while he and Isaac go up. "We will come back" can be read as faith or as kindness to the boy; Jubilees does not say.

settings.to: each other, alone on the way up
settings.when: as they climb with the fire, the knife and the wood
settings.why: Isaac sees everything but the animal. Abraham's answer, that the Lord will see to the lamb, turns into the name of the place (18:13).

settings.what: The Lord's order to the angel
settings.to: the angel of the presence, with Mastema standing by
settings.when: as Abraham reaches for the knife
settings.why: To stop the sacrifice once Abraham's fear of the Lord was proven before the accuser.

settings.what: The angel's call and the Lord's oath
settings.by: the angel of the presence, speaking in the Lord's name
settings.when: at the altar on the mountain
settings.why: To stop the knife, to renew the promises of offspring and blessing for the nations, and to declare that Abraham's faithfulness has been made known to all.

settings.what: The law of the seven-day festival
settings.by: the angel, quoting the heavenly tablets
settings.when: after the account of Abraham's return
settings.why: To give Israel a yearly festival rooted in Abraham's journey and to claim that it is written in heaven, not invented later.

title: Sarah's Grave and Jacob's Blessing
sum: Sarah dies in Hebron. Abraham buys the double cave from the sons of Heth and pays in full, though they offer it for nothing. The angels call this his tenth trial: he who had been promised the whole land did not say a word about the promise but begged for a grave. He was found faithful and written on the heavenly tablets as the friend of the Lord.

Isaac marries Rebekah, Abraham takes Keturah as a third wife, and Jacob and Esau are born. Jacob learns to write; Esau learns war. Abraham loves Jacob and sees that the promise runs through him. He tells Rebekah to watch over Jacob, and blesses Jacob with the blessings of Adam, Enoch, Noah and Shem.
readings: Read as a portrait of patience
The chapter's key words are patience and faithfulness. The burial scene of Genesis 23 becomes a test of whether Abraham will complain about God's slow promises (19:3, 9).
Read as the choice of Jacob
The second half explains in advance the stolen blessing of Genesis 27: Abraham himself chose Jacob, and charged Rebekah to guard him (19:16-21), so her later plan carries out his wish.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale as Scripture, together with the Orit (the books of Moses), where Genesis 23-25 tells of the same years.
views.H: Critics see the writer filling a gap in Genesis, where Abraham and Jacob never meet, to make Jacob Abraham's chosen heir. Jacob the scholar and Esau the warrior also reflect the book's values: learning, the law and the priestly line.
views.N: James 2:23 says Abraham "was called the friend of God", and Jubilees 19:9 is one of the oldest witnesses to that title. Hebrews 11:9-13 speaks of the patriarchs living as foreigners in the promised land and dying without receiving it, the very point of the burial test.
views.J: The ten trials are a rabbinic theme (Mishnah Avot 5:3). Charles notes that two medieval Jewish teachers, Jonah Girondi and Simon Duran, also made Sarah's burial the tenth, while Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer ends with the binding of Isaac. The Targums have Jacob study in a school, as Jubilees has him learn to write.
views.W: Most churches read the friend-of-God title and the faith of Abraham from Genesis, 2 Chronicles 20:7, Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23, and see Jubilees as an early Jewish echo of them.

deep.b: Genesis 23 is a long, polite bargaining scene. Jubilees shortens it to a few verses and adds one sentence of meaning: "He did not say a single word about the promise of the land" (19:9). The man promised all of Canaan had to ask for a grave in it and pay full price. That, the book says, was his last and tenth trial, and his patience earned him the name "friend of the Lord". Stephen makes a similar point in Acts 7:5: God gave Abraham "not even a foot of ground" in the land.

By Genesis's own numbers, Abraham lived until Jacob and Esau were fifteen, but Genesis never brings them together. Jubilees uses those years. Abraham watches Esau's deeds, recognizes the chosen heir in Jacob (19:16), and puts Rebekah in charge of him (19:17-21). The blessing of 19:27-29 hands down the blessings of the first fathers, and the next chapters build to Abraham's death with Jacob in his arms (23:1-3).

echoes: Genesis 23:1-20; Genesis 24:15; Genesis 25:1-6; Genesis 25:20-28; 2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23; Acts 7:5; Hebrews 11:9-13; Deuteronomy 7:6

settings.when: while Jacob and Esau were young men, after Abraham saw Esau's deeds
settings.why: To place Jacob in Rebekah's care as the heir of the promise. For readers of Genesis 27 it justifies in advance her help in getting Jacob the blessing.
To hand on the blessings of Adam, Enoch, Noah and Shem and to promise that the spirits of Mastema will not rule Jacob's line.

title: Abraham's Charge to All His Sons
sum: Abraham gathers all his descendants: Ishmael and his twelve sons, Isaac and his two sons, Keturah's six sons and their sons. He commands them to keep the way of the Lord, love their neighbors, circumcise their sons and keep away from sexual sin and impurity. A woman who commits sexual sin is to be burned, and no one is to marry the daughters of Canaan.

He reminds them of the judgment of the giants and of Sodom, warns them against idols, and promises the blessings of rain, crops and herds if they serve the Most High God. Then he gives them gifts and sends them away from Isaac. Ishmael's and Keturah's sons settle the eastern desert and become the Arabs and Ishmaelites.
readings: Read as a farewell testament

This is the first of three farewell speeches (20; 21; 22), in the style of Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49) and Moses' farewell (Deuteronomy 31-33). Each moves from general to narrower: here all the sons, then Isaac, then Jacob.
Read as a law for the nations
Abraham charges even the non-Israelite sons with circumcision, sexual purity and the rejection of idols. The book holds that these laws bind all Abraham's family.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale, this testament included, as Scripture, together with the Orit (the books of Moses).
views.H: Critics read the speech as aimed at the writer's own time: Jews who married their pagan neighbors or adopted Greek ways. The harsh law of 20:4 differs from the Torah's (Charles), which suggests a group with its own strict reading of the law.
views.N: The pairing of the giants and Sodom as warnings (20:5) appears again in Jude 6-7 and 2 Peter 2:4-6. The ban on idols and sexual sin for Abraham's non-Israelite sons is like the rules the Jerusalem council gave Gentile believers in Acts 15:20, 29.
views.J: Charles notes that the Talmud (Sanhedrin 59b) debated whether circumcision bound the sons of Ishmael and Keturah.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early Jewish moral sermon in Abraham's name, not as Scripture. On its burning penalty, which Charles shows differs from the Torah's, see the section below.

deep.h: A penalty the Torah does not give
deep.b: "If any woman or girl among you commits sexual sin, burn her with fire" (20:4). Charles notes that in Leviticus and Deuteronomy the penalty for adultery is death by stoning (Deuteronomy 22:23-24), and burning is only for a priest's daughter who sins sexually (Leviticus 21:9). The closest parallel is Judah's order about Tamar (Genesis 38:24), which Jubilees retells in chapter 41. Jubilees thus goes beyond, and conflicts with, the written law. For Christian readers, Jesus' answer to a woman caught in adultery (John 8:7-11, a passage whose place in John is debated) stands against it.

echoes: Genesis 18:19; Genesis 25:1-6; Genesis 25:12-18; Leviticus 21:9; Deuteronomy 7:13; Exodus 20:4-5; Exodus 23:25; Jude 6-7; 2 Peter 2:4-6; Acts 15:20

settings.what: Abraham's testament to all his descendants
settings.to: Ishmael and his twelve sons, Isaac and his two sons, Keturah's six sons and their sons
settings.when: in the year before his death, before sending the others away (20:11)
settings.why: To bind every branch of his family to the way of the Lord: justice, love of neighbor, circumcision, sexual purity, no Canaanite wives and no idols. Knowing that the hearers include the ancestors of the Arabs shows that the book saw these as family laws, not Israel's alone.

title: The Priestly Law Handed to Isaac
sum: Abraham, now old, calls Isaac and gives him his own testament. He speaks of a life spent remembering the Lord and hating idols, and of a God who is holy and takes no bribes. Then the speech becomes a manual for a priest: no eating blood; how to offer the peace offering and its fat; eating the meat within two days; salt on every offering; which woods may be burned on the altar, and in what condition; washing before and after sacrifice; covering spilled blood.

He ends with the law of blood for blood: no payment may buy off a killing, since only the killer's blood cleans the earth. He warns Isaac against the ways of humankind and blesses him: God will raise from him the plant of righteousness.
readings: Read as priestly law before Sinai
Abraham teaches Leviticus to Isaac. Jubilees claims that the sacrificial law was known and kept from the first fathers, written in their books (21:10), and only later given to Moses.
Read as a father's last words
The chapter begins and ends as a farewell (21:1-2, 25-26). The long middle is the inheritance Abraham most wants to leave: right worship.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale, these laws of sacrifice included, as Scripture, together with the Orit (the books of Moses).
views.H: Critics see the concerns of a priestly circle of the 100s BC: correct wood, correct washing, correct times. Charles shows the same rules in the Testament of Levi 9, handed from Isaac to Levi, and judged that the Testament used Jubilees or a shared source.
views.N: The blood rule (21:6, 18) stands behind the blood rule of Acts 15:20. Hebrews 9-10 reads the whole sacrificial system as a shadow fulfilled in Christ's one offering. "A sin that leads to death" (21:22) is close to 1 John 5:16.
views.J: Rabbinic law has its own rules for the altar. Charles notes that the Mishnah (Tamid 2:3) allows any wood except olive and vine, while Jubilees approves olive and lists only certain evergreens.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early Jewish witness to how sacrifice was understood, with no authority of its own. On whether the blood rules still apply, see the card at Leviticus 17.

deep.b: In Genesis, Abraham builds altars and sacrifices, but the rules of sacrifice come at Sinai. Jubilees puts them in Abraham's mouth: the peace offering with its fat and kidneys (Leviticus 3:3-4), the two-day limit for eating (Leviticus 19:6), salt (Leviticus 2:13), washing (Exodus 30:19-21), covering blood (Leviticus 17:13), and blood for blood (Numbers 35:33). He even says he found them "in the book of my forefathers, in the words of Enoch and in the words of Noah" (21:10). Charles notes that no such law book of Enoch survives. The claim fits the whole book: the law is eternal, written on the heavenly tablets, and the patriarchs already lived by it.

21:12-14 gives a list of woods that may be burned, and rules that they be fresh, whole and fragrant. The names are partly Greek (cypress, pine, cedar, myrtle, laurel) and partly obscure. Charles noted a list of fourteen evergreens in the Greek farming book Geoponica, and that 1 Enoch 3:1 speaks of fourteen trees that keep their leaves. The Testament of Levi 9 has Isaac tell Levi to offer "twelve trees always in leaf", as Abraham taught him. The concern is that what goes up to God should be clean and give a pleasing smell.

echoes: Leviticus 3:1-17; Leviticus 2:13; Leviticus 7:15-18; Leviticus 17:10-14; Exodus 30:19-21; Numbers 35:31-34; Genesis 9:4-6; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 12:23; 1 John 5:16; Acts 15:20

settings.when: in Abraham's last year, at a hundred and seventy-five
settings.why: To hand on to Isaac, the heir, the rules of right worship and the law of blood, so that the family's sacrifices would be acceptable and its line kept from destruction. For Isaac, who will offer at Abraham's altar (22:3), the law is practical: this is how to be the family's priest.
settings.readers: Charles judged that the Testament of Levi 9, where Isaac hands the same priestly rules to Levi "as Abraham also taught me", used this chapter or a source shared with it.

title: The Last Feast and the Blessing of Jacob
sum: In the year he dies, Abraham's sons come to keep the Feast of Weeks with him. Isaac offers a burnt offering and a peace offering, Rebekah sends new bread from the first fruits, and Abraham eats, drinks and thanks God for a life of peace.

Then he calls Jacob, kisses him and blesses him at length: may God choose him and his offspring, make them holy and rule the nations through them. He warns Jacob to separate from the nations, not to eat with them, not to take a Canaanite wife, and to have nothing to do with idols, the dead and demons. He gives Jacob his house, and that night the old man and the boy sleep together on one bed.
readings: Read as a passing of the torch
The blessing skips Isaac and goes straight to Jacob, the grandson who will become Israel. Abraham's house, his blessing and his commands all pass to Jacob in one night.
Read as a manifesto of separation
22:16-22 is the book's strongest call to keep apart from Gentiles. Charles saw in it the pressures of the Maccabean age, when a Greek king forced Jews to eat unclean food.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale as Scripture, together with the Orit (the books of Moses); this chapter's feast, blessing and death scene fill the years before Genesis 25:7-10.
views.H: Critics read 22:16-22 as aimed at Jews who ate with Gentiles, married them or joined in their worship, in the decades of Greek rule and the Maccabean revolt.
views.N: The separation of 22:16 is the very issue of Acts 10:28, Acts 11:3 and Galatians 2:11-14, where Peter's table fellowship with Gentiles is challenged and Paul defends it. Christian readers see the gospel answering this chapter's wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14).
views.J: Jewish law kept rules about Gentile food and wine for its own reasons; Jubilees is an early and extreme form. The Feast of Weeks as the family's covenant feast fits the book's own calendar (6:17-22).
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a witness to the Judaism the early church grew up in, and to the barrier the gospel crossed. They do not hold its blanket condemnation of Canaan's descendants (22:21).

deep.b: "Separate yourself from the nations, and do not eat with them" (22:16). The reasons follow: the nations offer sacrifices to the dead, bow to demons, eat among the graves and say to wood "You are my God" (22:17-18). Charles linked the passage to the time when Antiochus IV tried to make Jews eat unclean food (1 Maccabees 1:47-48; 2 Maccabees 6:18-21). In the New Testament, the same rule meets the gospel: Peter tells Cornelius that a Jew does not mix with foreigners, until God showed him otherwise (Acts 10:28), and Paul opposes Peter at Antioch for drawing back from Gentile tables (Galatians 2:11-14).

deep.h: Canaan and the day of judgment
deep.b: 22:20-22 says no one born from Canaan "will be saved on the day of judgment". Genesis curses Canaan (Genesis 9:25), but the Bible also tells of Canaanites saved: Rahab (Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5) and the Canaanite woman whose daughter Jesus healed (Matthew 15:22-28). Here Jubilees goes beyond the Bible and, on this point, conflicts with it.

echoes: Genesis 27:27-29; Genesis 49:26; Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:15-21; Deuteronomy 32:8-9; Isaiah 52:11; Jeremiah 2:27; Acts 10:28; Galatians 2:11-14; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Luke 16:22

settings.when: after eating the first fruits of the Feast of Weeks, in the year of his death
settings.why: To thank God for a long life of peace and to pray that his descendants become God's chosen people.

settings.what: Abraham's blessing and charge to Jacob
settings.when: the same feast, in his last days
settings.why: To make Jacob heir of the promises and of Abraham's house, and to warn him to keep apart from the nations and their idols. The hearer is Israel's own ancestor, so every Jewish reader is meant to hear the charge as his own.
settings.readers: Charles held that "the very existence of Judaism in 200-150 B.C. made such exclusiveness indispensable", and set beside the rule against eating with Gentiles (22:16) the attempt of Antiochus IV to force Jews to eat unclean food (1 Maccabees 1:47-48; 2 Maccabees 6:18-21).

settings.to: God, with Jacob in his arms
settings.when: the last night of his life
settings.why: To commit Jacob to God's mercy and covenant forever.

title: Abraham's Death and the Last Days
sum: Abraham places Jacob's fingers on his eyes, blesses God and dies in the night with Jacob still in his arms. Jacob wakes to find him cold, the household weeps, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah. He lived a hundred and seventy-five years, less than four jubilees.

That fact turns into a vision. The ancients lived nearly a thousand years; after the Flood lives shrank, and even righteous Abraham grew old early. An evil generation will come, full of sickness and disaster, in which the young accuse the old of forsaking the covenant and the calendar, blood is shed, the holy place is defiled, and cruel nations invade. Then the children will begin to study the law, lives will lengthen again toward a thousand years, there will be no satan, and the righteous will rejoice while their bones rest in the earth.
readings: Read as history in the form of prophecy

Charles, following Bousset, read 23:16-31 as a veiled account of the writer's own time: the rise of the pious Hasideans, the Maccabean wars, the strife with the Hellenizers, and invasions by Syria. On this reading the vision dates the book to the second century BC.
Read as a vision of the last days

Many readers take the passage as a general picture of the end, built from the prophets (Isaiah 65:17-25; Hosea 4:3; Jeremiah 6:23), like the woes of Matthew 24 and the visions of 4 Ezra. Its turning point is repentance and the study of the law.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads Kufale as Scripture, the account of what was shown to Moses on Sinai, so it receives this vision as part of that revelation.
views.H: This chapter is the main key for dating Jubilees. Charles placed it in the 100s BC by matching 23:16-23 with 1 Maccabees.
views.N: The woes of 23:13-23, the strife between young and old (23:16, 19) and "no satan" (23:29) are part of the Jewish background of Matthew 24, Luke 12:53 and Revelation 20:2-3. Paul's "sinners from the Gentiles" (Galatians 2:15) uses the same idiom as 23:23-24.
views.J: The chapter links Psalm 90:10 with the shortening of life since the Flood and hopes for a return to the years of Adam.
views.W: Most churches read the vision as an early Jewish hope, useful for understanding New Testament teaching about the last days, but not as a map of the future. Its view of the afterlife in 23:31 is debated.

deep.b: The book counts ages in jubilees. The first fathers lived nineteen jubilees (931 years, close to Adam's 930, Genesis 5:5). After the Flood, life spans fall (Genesis 11), and Abraham did not reach four jubilees. Soon, the vision says, people will grow old before two jubilees, and a man of a jubilee and a half (about seventy-four years) will be called old: Psalm 90:10's seventy or eighty (23:12, 15). The book explains the decline by trouble and wickedness (23:9). In the renewal, lives will grow again toward a thousand years (23:27), the age Adam would have reached without sin (4:29-30), like Isaiah 65:20.

deep.h: Bones at rest, spirits in joy
deep.b: 23:31 is the clearest statement in Jubilees about what happens to the righteous after death: "Their bones will rest in the earth, and their spirits will have much joy." Charles read it as teaching no resurrection of the body but a blessed immortality of the spirit, and called it the earliest instance of that hope in the last two centuries BC, found next in 1 Enoch 91-104. He weighed the other reading of "they will rise up" in 23:30: if it meant that the righteous are raised to share in the kingdom, this book would separate the resurrection from the final judgment. He judged that the words "apparently" do not refer to resurrection but mean that the servants become strong when the Lord heals them (23:29, "days of blessing and healing"). The text itself affirms only two things: the bodies of the righteous rest, and their spirits rejoice.

Charles matched the vision with the history of the 160s BC: the "sons" who accuse their fathers (23:16) are the Hasideans; the armed attempt to turn people back to the way (23:20) is Judas Maccabeus; those who "name the great name" falsely and defile the holiest place (23:21) are the Hellenizing priests under Alcimus; and the cruel nations of 23:23 are the Syrian armies. He compared 1 Enoch 90:6-7, where lambs are born who open their eyes.

echoes: Genesis 25:7-10; Genesis 50:1; Psalm 90:10; Isaiah 65:17-25; Hosea 4:3; Jeremiah 8:2; Daniel 12:2; Matthew 24:6-29; Galatians 2:15; Revelation 20:2-3; 1 Enoch 90:6-7; 1 Maccabees 1:43-45

settings.what: The vision of shrinking lives and the last days
settings.when: after telling of Abraham's death at a hundred and seventy-five
settings.why: To explain why lives grew short, to warn of a coming evil generation that forsakes the covenant and the calendar, and to promise renewal when the young return to the law. Inside the story Moses is told to write it down as a testimony.
settings.readers: Charles read 23:16-23 as the Maccabean struggle of the 160s BC, and dated the book between 135 BC, when John Hyrcanus became high priest, and 96 BC, before the Pharisees broke openly with the Maccabean rulers. On his reading the first readers lived under the later Maccabean high priests, a generation or more after the events the vision describes.
